h1: Olive Oil for Hummus: In the Blend and On Top
excerpt: A bowl of hummus takes oil twice, and the two pours do different work. Which oil belongs in the blend, which belongs on the surface, how much of each, and how to serve it so the oil sits in a pool instead of vanishing.
keyTakeaway: Hummus takes oil twice. About thirty millilitres goes into the blend, where tahini and lemon mask most of its character, so the everyday bottle is enough there. The pour on top is tasted almost neat, a tablespoon a portion, and that is where the better extra virgin belongs.
heroAlt: A ceramic bowl of hummus with a pool of green olive oil in the middle and whole chickpeas scattered on the table beside it.
inlineAlt: A farmer pouring olive oil from a dark bottle into a stoneware bowl on a wooden table
intro: Most recipes mention olive oil once. A bowl of hummus takes it twice, and the two pours do different work: one disappears into the paste, the other is eaten almost neat.
Hummus is a Levantine dish and this oil is pressed in Palestine, which is the whole of that context. The rest is method.

blocks.text: Oil goes into the blend, and oil goes onto the finished bowl. Inside, it is a texture ingredient that works into the tahini and chickpea paste and disappears. On top it is a condiment, tasted almost neat, one mouthful at a time.
That decides where the money goes. Oil blended into tahini, lemon and garlic loses to three louder flavours. The pour sits on the surface with nothing in front of it.

Use the plainer oil where it will be masked and the one you would happily taste on bread where it will be tasted. A mild everyday oil does honest work in the blend. The extra virgin goes on last, off the blade.
A long, fast blend can sharpen an extra virgin's bitterness, another reason the good oil goes on by hand. Both sizes are on the [products page](/products).

A household batch starts from 250 g of dried chickpeas soaked overnight, which cook down to roughly 600 g; two and a half drained 400 g tins land in the same place. Everything below scales off that weight and makes six generous portions.

sections.heading: Tahini and lemon set the balance

blocks.text: Oil cannot rescue a badly balanced bowl. Tahini brings weight and a faint bitterness, lemon cuts it, salt makes both legible. Get those three right while the machine is running, because once the dip is smooth the only things left are temperature and the pour.

items: **Thick and bitter:** more lemon, 15 ml at a time.
**Sharp and thin:** more tahini, then a pinch of salt.
**Flat:** salt first, not lemon. Under-salted hummus reads sour.
**Stiff:** iced water by the spoon. Oil loosens it heavily.

sections.heading: Why fridge-cold hummus tastes of nothing

blocks.text: Straight from the fridge, hummus is stiff and mute, and cold oil poured onto a cold surface sits in a sluggish film instead of spreading. Take the bowl out twenty to thirty minutes before anyone eats; in an air-conditioned kitchen, give it thirty.
Never warm the oil to speed that up; heat strips an extra virgin of the aroma you paid for, as [olive oil for bread and dipping](/blog/olive-oil-for-bread-and-dipping) sets out.

sections.heading: Serving it so the oil pools rather than soaks

blocks.text: A pool of green oil in the middle of a smooth surface is not decoration. It is how the oil reaches the mouth in a quantity you can taste. Spread the dip flat in a deep bowl and the pour vanishes within a minute.

items: Use a wide, shallow dish; depth swallows the pour.
Smooth the top with the back of a spoon. Peaks drink oil.
Turn a slow spiral from the centre outward, leaving a channel.
Pour into the channel, a tablespoon a portion, and stop.
Do not stir it in. Scatter chickpeas or za'atar around the pool.
Leave the bottle out for the second pour.

blocks.text: An infused oil works here too, one flavour at a time: wild thyme or blackseed, poured at the table. More in [Palestinian olive oil](/blog/palestinian-olive-oil-what-makes-it-different).
Thirty millilitres of the everyday oil in the blend, a tablespoon of the good one on top, and the bowl out of the fridge half an hour early.

faqs.q: Should olive oil go inside hummus or only on top?
faqs.a: Both, in different amounts. About 30 ml goes into the blend for texture, where tahini and lemon mask it. The pour on top is what anyone actually tastes, so use the better bottle there.

faqs.q: How much olive oil goes into a batch of hummus?
faqs.a: For a batch built on 250 g of dried chickpeas, about 30 ml inside the blend and roughly 15 ml poured over each portion at the table. Across a platter the pour is the larger share.

faqs.q: Which olive oil is best for hummus?
faqs.a: An extra virgin with a green, peppery character for the pour, because it is tasted almost neat. A milder everyday oil is enough for the blend, where tahini and lemon cover it.

faqs.q: Why does the olive oil sink into my hummus?
faqs.a: Either the surface is rough or the dish is too deep. Smooth the top with the back of a spoon, turn a shallow spiral into it, and pour into that channel.

faqs.q: Should hummus be served cold or at room temperature?
faqs.a: At room temperature. Straight from the fridge it is stiff and its flavour is muted, and cold oil spreads badly on a cold surface. Twenty to thirty minutes out is usually enough.

faqs.q: Can I use an infused olive oil on hummus?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is one of the easiest places to use one. Wild thyme or blackseed sit naturally on hummus. Use a single flavour, poured at the table rather than blended in.
